articles.content: Refundable charge intended to discourage time wasters from filing applications that will never be realized Dan Robinson Dan Robinson IT INFRASTRUCTURE REPORTER Published fri 31 Jul 2026 // 10:15 UTC Ofgem is seeking feedback on proposals to levy a fee on datacenter development projects at the time they apply for a grid connection. The move aims to discourage companies from seeking approval for speculative applications that clog up the pipeline and cause connection delays, without ever resulting in finished datacenters. The UK regulator for electricity and gas says connection applications for electrical supply have surged from 41 gigawatts (GW) to 125 GW in under a year, with datacenters accounting for at least 80 GW of the new demand. Even before that happened, one of the UK's big developers complained that its build teams faced a wait of "a number of years" for work such as local substation upgrades to increase grid capacity. Ofgem is proposing a Datacenter Commitment Fee paid by the developers of large server farm projects when accepting a grid connection offer. The fee would be refunded once the facility is drawing power, or forfeited if the project exits the queue early instead. Alan Howard, Omdia principal analyst for Colocation and DC Building,  told us previously that the power connection queue issue is a big problem, not just for the UK, but also in the US and other markets around the globe. "The strategy for many datacenter operators is to secure multiple land parcel rights, request a grid load connection for each (often requiring a costly load study), and see what gets approved so they can build. The capital investment to take all these projects seriously is clearly untenable and a huge financial risk for the energy sector if the demand doesn't fully materialize," he said. Trump expands voluntary pledge to keep datacenter costs off household power bills Australia demands AI companies must produce more energy than they consume, stop ‘theft’ of content New York becomes first state to halt datacenter buildouts Amazon's European datacenter buildout blows a breaker as grid connection wait list hits 7 years The issue is therefore that developers apply in multiple locations to secure power for a single campus, fill up the national application pipeline with speculative requests and hold up the works for viable projects. “Britain's electricity demand connections queue has more than tripled in size in less than a year, and consumers should not bear the risks created by speculative projects taking up space in the system,” said Eleanor Warburton, the regulator’s director for Energy System Design and Development. Ofgem’s suggestion is that the fee should be set within a proposed range of £237,500 ($319k) to £712,500 ($957k) per megawatt, which it believes is equivalent to about 2.5 percent to 7.5 percent of average project costs. It is suggests developers demonstrate progress with their project if they wish to retain their place in the queue, meeting criteria such as financial capability, commercial maturity and procurement activity milestones. Global colocation biz Telehouse, which operates five datacenters in the London area, told The Register it supports measures to ensure grid capacity is prioritized for credible project, though it has some reservations. “Ofgem’s proposal is an important initiative, but it must be implemented in a way that maintains the UK’s attractiveness as a destination for AI and digital infrastructure investment,” said Telehouse Europe, managing director, Mark Pestridge. “A refundable fee-based approach should not deter serious investors, but create a more transparent connections process that gives viable projects greater certainty.” However, reforming the queue will not resolve the underlying capacity challenge, Telehouse points out - the need to expand the grid and make more energy available. “A long-term solution will require sustained investment in the grid, alongside much closer collaboration between datacenter operators, local councils, National Grid and network operators at the earliest stages of planning,” Pestridge said. “Better coordination and forecasting will help ensure infrastructure is developed in the right places, at the right time, and that viable projects do not continue to face delays even after speculative demand has been removed.” The finger of blame for all this bother can be pointed at the government, which unveiled its AI Opportunities Action Plan at the start of last year. This included plans for “AI Growth Zones" with streamlined planning processes to speed along the building of more datacenters, apparently without bothering to check if the electricity infrastructure was ready. To try to tackle the bottleneck, the government set up an AI Energy Council, bringing together energy industry representatives and major technology firms to thrash out a strategy, co-chaired by the former Technology Secretary and Energy Secretary. The Register reported on the challenges faced last year. Ofgem’s consultation is open to anyone with an interest, and closes on September 16, 2026.  The agency has response templates available on its website here . ® energy datacenters ai uk ofgem systems

articles.title: FCC Rule Threatens Smart Appliances with WiFi Restrictions
articles.content: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story US Federal Communications Commission banned the import of foreign-made advanced mobile robots. Humanoid and quadruped robots are specifically named, indicating the true target is robotic versions of people and animals, but something else happens to be an “advanced mobile robot”: robot vacuums . So what does this ban mean? Though it's effective immediately, nothing changes for now. Robot vacuums won't get removed from the market, and your current robot vacuum won't stop working. The ban will instead stop new models from getting FCC approval to be sold in the United States. The vacuums available now won't be affected, but new models likely won't make it to the US if they're manufactured outside the country. And, unfortunately, a lot of great robot vacuum brands aren't based in the States. Here's everything to know about what will happen next. What the Ban Covers The FCC updated its Covered List this week to include foreign-made advanced mobile robots, which include robot vacuums. The Covered List, which comes from Section 2 of the Secure and Trusted Communications Networks Act of 2019 , is a “list of communications equipment and services that are deemed to pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States or the security and safety of United States persons.” It may feel like overkill for just a robot vacuum, but the definition of an advanced robotic device from the National Security Determination , an interagency body of the Executive Branch, clearly includes them. That definition includes the following highlights: Autonomous mobile robots that are capable of locomotion, obstacle avoidance, navigation, or movement on the ground; Operates at a distance from a human operator or supervisor; Combined weight of the device and docking station is over 4.4 pounds; Contains a sensor capable of perceiving its environment; Contains a component capable of providing network connectivity, including Bluetooth and Wi-Fi; Contains software running locally or remotely, including firmware and AI or machine-learning; model weights that control the robot's navigation and movement perception. The National Security Determination said that connected vehicles, vehicles on rail lines, aircraft, and unmanned underwater vehicles are not included in the ban, along with stationary robots. But foreign-made robot vacuums , along with similar robots like robotic pool cleaners and automated lawn mowers , look to be on the chopping block. The announcement comes after the FCC labeled all of these devices a security risk, since, according to the National Security Determination , “the networked capabilities of advanced robotic systems create extensive vulnerabilities and vectors for attacks that can manipulate the data and physical operation of the advanced robotic system.” The concern is primarily with the cameras and sensors built into these devices—some even have microphones built into the base station for voice commands. It is a security risk to bring any device into your home that has a camera and the ability to connect to the internet—especially if your Wi-Fi isn't secure . But it's interesting to see the ban stop at robot vacuums and not, say, smart speakers or devices with always-on cameras. The FCC documentation actually lists live cameras as an example, as well as an example of a humanoid robot being hacked, but no example for robot vacuums. , so we might continue to see bans for various household technology products roll out as the year goes on. What Happens Now? Robot Vacuums That Don’t Suck (Unless It’s Dirt) Tired of vacuuming? Hand the reins to a robot vacuum. By Nena Farrell For now, you can shop robot vacuums (and other, similar automated home cleaning robots) as you normally would. FCC approval has already been given to all the robots on the market, so we can expect changes to take place in the future rather than immediately. I reached out to the makers of my top robot vacuum picks, Shark and Eufy, along with popular robot makers Dreame and Roborock. Shark and Dreame didn't respond, and Roborock declined to comment. Eufy replied with the following statement: “We are aware of the FCC’s recent update. Based on our current understanding, the new rule does not affect the continued availability, use, or support of products we currently sell in the United States. Those products remain available and will continue to receive updates and customer support.” So don't worry about getting rid of your robot vacuum if you already have one you love. If you're in the market for a new model, I'd recommend shopping the newest models from brands that could be affected, like Dreame and Eufy, in case future models are blocked from arriving in the States. It will also be interesting to see which companies avoid the ban— Shark is based in the US, for example, but it's unclear where the company's robot manufacturing is located. Matic is another US-based brand that could potentially evade the ban. But the buying options will be much, much more limited as time goes on. The ban is disappointing news with IFA Berlin starting September 4, where we often see new robot vacuums announced. I'm not sure anything we'll see there this year will reach the US. A reduced market also isn't good for consumers—having fewer options never helps a category and might ultimately raise prices on less powerful vacuums because of limited supply. Only time will tell what the fallout will be. Power up with unlimited access to WIRED . Get best-in-class reporting and exclusive subscriber content that's too important to ignore. Subscribe Today .

articles.title: AI Scammers Outperform Humans in Trust Building
articles.content: • Company Offering Printed Books to Train AI Stops After 404 Media Coverage · Jul 31, 2026 at 10:04 AM Citing backlash, ISBNdb removed its webpages about training AI, denied ever buying, scanning, or selling a book for AI training, and said the site was a "test of market interest." Priscilla Du Preez 🇨🇦 / Unsplash Following 404 Media’s reporting that book database company ISBNdb claimed to source printed books to then sell to AI companies for AI training, the company deleted the part of its website offering the service and walked back claims that it would train AI models, and instead called it “a test of market interest.”  On July 30, nine days after 404 Media’s reporting, ISBNdb added a note to its homepage and an update on its news page about the change. “We've seen the recent coverage about a marketing landing page on our site, and we understand the concern it raised. The facts: ISBNdb has never purchased, scanned, or sold a book — for AI training or anything else,” ISBNdb wrote. “We don't train AI models, and we never have. The page was a test of market interest; no such service was ever brought to life. We've taken the page down. Our job is helping people find books. For more than two decades, ISBNdb has been the card catalog of the book world — the data behind how bookstores, libraries, and reading apps connect readers with titles. Data about books, not the books themselves. That hasn't changed.”  ISBNdb removed the landing page for “Printed Books Sourcing for Your AI LLMs Dataset Needs” on July 28. “It was part of exploring demand, and we've chosen to pivot away from that direction. Our main ISBNdb (book metadata API) services are unaffected and running as usual,” the site says.  ISBNdb replied to 404 Media's request for comment about the removed pages with the same note that's now on the homepage. The company has not replied to 404 Media's previous attempts to reach it for comment. AI Companies Are Buying Tons of Old Books Because They’re Free of AI Slop ISBNdb, a company that sources printed books for AI companies to turn into training data, tells clients “the optics problem is real.” Emanuel Maiberg In one now-removed article on its site , ISBNdb said that printed books published before 2022 are ideal for AI training data because they don’t include AI generated text, and ingesting these books could prevent model collapse. The article also suggested that book authors who might be opposed to this use of their work could just write with manipulating and sabotaging AI models in mind.  404 Media spoke to booksellers and saw reports online detailing a sudden uptick in sales recently. “It's not just the quantity, but the weirdness of the orders,” one bookseller told 404 Media. “The type of books [...] there's no rhyme or reason to it. Also, there's a total disregard for the price of the book. I've had some books that sold through this way that were [...] greatly overpriced. That's kind of a tell for AI because they have just so much money.”  “Purchasing paper books at scale from the secondary market does not deprive any creator of income they would otherwise have received,” one of ISBNdb’s now-removed pages said. “These are books that have already fully discharged their financial obligation to their creators.”  In January, book authors filed a copyright lawsuit against Anthropic, revealing internal documents that showed Anthropic planned to obtain and scan millions of printed books and destroy them in the process. An investigation by the Washington Post found that Anthropic was buying books from a company called Better World Books, one of several marketplaces where libraries, retailers, and individuals sell books.   In ISBNdb’s now-removed marketing materials, it admitted that getting caught destroying printed books during the scanning process would not be a good look. “The optics problem is real,” ISBNdb’s site said . “‘AI company destroys two million books’ is not a headline that generates sympathy.” Emanuel Maiberg contributed reporting to this story. articles.content: Advertisement Google World United States & Canada Google rolls back new satellite image AI tool after backlash Experts warn it could produce realistic geospatial fakes for misinformation, such as images of explosions, nuclear sites and militant bases 3 -MIN READ 3 -MIN Listen Agence France-Presse Published: 5:16am, 1 Aug 2026 Updated: 5:49am, 1 Aug 2026 Google rolled back a new feature on Friday that allowed Google Earth users to generate AI visualisations on top of the service’s satellite imagery, following a furious backlash from researchers and open-source intelligence experts about the potential for disinformation. “We’ve seen geospatial professionals using this feature for a range of useful purposes, however we’ve also seen people sharing screenshots of generated imagery that appear to violate our policies,” a Google spokesman said in a statement. “So we’re rolling back this feature in Google Earth while we work on implementing stronger guardrails.” “We know that people uniquely trust Google Earth for a reliable view of the world,” the statement added. The “create image” tool, unveiled Thursday, had integrated Google’s Nano Banana 2 image-generation technology into Google Earth, letting users zoom into locations and build pictures in seconds based on the program’s satellite, aerial and 3D-mapping data. Trust in satellite imagery has taken decades to build and could be irrevocably damaged overnight Ross Burley, Centre for Information Resilience executive director Google had described it as a way to “visualise history, create real estate plans and more”. articles.title: Musk's Super PAC Pledges $100M to Republicans in 8 States
articles.content: Musk’s super PAC to pour at least $100M backing Republicans in 8 states by Miranda Nazzaro - 07/30/26 4:42 PM ET Link copied - 07/30/26 4:42 PM ET Link copied NOW PLAYING Elon Musk is jumping back into the political spending arena ahead of the 2026 midterms with a new field program to help elect Republicans in at least eight states. The Tesla and SpaceX CEO authorized his super PAC, America PAC, to spend $100 million to $120 million for a new field program focused on conservative voter turnout in the 2026 midterms, The New York Times reported Thursday, citing two anonymous sources briefed on the plans. America PAC poured more than $250 million into Trump’s reelection campaign in 2024, making Musk the biggest political donor in U.S. history. America PAC is reviving these spending efforts and has communicated with other Republicans in recent weeks about the new field initiative, the Times reported. The effort is reportedly being coordinated with other GOP spending groups, as well. The targeted Senate races include Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan and Ohio, while conversations are also being held over races in North Carolina, Georgia and Texas, The New York Times added. The super PAC will also reportedly spend in House races in Washington, Wisconsin and California. It comes one day after Axios first reported the resurgence of America PAC’s efforts and its focus on boosting Republican voter turnout in a non-presidential election cycle. A spokesperson for America PAC did not comment on the Times’s report, but they confirmed the Axios report to The Hill, stating the spending group is “excited” to contribute to Republicans’ efforts to keep their majority in Congress this fall. “The president’s political team and the rest of the GOP apparatus have built a top-notch operation that will put Republicans in a strong position to buck history and retain control of Congress this fall, and we’re excited to again be part of the team,” wrote Andrew Romeo, a spokesperson for America PAC, in a statement. The initiative will focus on door-knocking, mail, and digital advertisements targeting Republican voters, freeing up other groups to focus on television ads. The reports come just days after Musk told The Economist he “got carried away” with his brief venture into politics. The SpaceX CEO jumped into the political world during the 2024 elections, pouring hundreds of millions into the presidential race for Trump, while joining the then-candidate on the campaign trail. Musk led Trump’s cost-cutting effort known as the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), which involved sweeping job and funding cuts across the federal government. The efforts sparked controversy for Musk and his companies, including Tesla, which saw its stock drastically fall during his time in politics. Musk departed the White House in late May 2025, and DOGE officially shut down operations on July 4. Shortly after leaving government, Musk and Trump clashed in a public dispute over the president’s sweeping spending bill, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. During the feud, Musk threatened to launch a third party, but the effort never came to fruition. Musk and the president appeared to mend fences last year, with the tech billionaire most recently joining Trump on a trip to China with other tech leaders in May. articles.title: South African City Blames Telkom Cutoffs on 'Service Provider Migration'
articles.content: Residents face cascading service failures as the City of Joburg’s Telkom blackout and dual labour disputes at Johannesburg Water and Pikitup hinder emergency escalation and routine municipal repairs. By Anna Cox 30 Jul 2026 Illustrative image: City blames ’service provider migration’ for Telkom mobile and landline cutoffs as double labour crisis hits. (Photo: Generated by ChatGPT) | Telephone handset receivers. (Photo: Freepik) Dive Deeper Speed Read Summary Listen Dive Deeper The City of Joburg is attempting to downplay a severe Telkom blackout involving landlines and cellphones across municipal departments, claiming that only cellphones are not working because of a ‘routine service provider migration’ while falsely insisting landlines are unaffected. Addressing days of growing public frustration, the City broke its silence on Thursday, denying claims of non-payment and attributing the dead mobile lines to a contractual service provider roll-out. “The City of Johannesburg wishes to advise staff and residents that some officials’ municipal mobile line services are currently experiencing temporary disruptions as a result of the contractual transition from one mobile service provider to another,” the City said in an official media release. “The disruption primarily affects selected direct mobile lines used by individual City officials. Importantly, the City’s primary landlines and customer-facing channels, including the Joburg Call Centre, Customer Service Centres and emergency contact services, remain operational and available to residents.” However, direct testing conducted by Daily Maverick exposed a distinct operational split: while emergency dispatch lines (011 375) remain live, the metro’s primary administrative trunking network (011 407) – which connects the public, councillors, and senior municipal officials at Metro Centre and departmental desks – was completely unresponsive. Dead lines, disconnect messages Callers attempting to reach corporate lines across the 011 407 ranges were met only with dead lines and automated disconnect messages. While the functional 011 375 emergency call centre allows the City to claim that public-facing channels are operational, the blackout across 011 407 administrative extensions leaves ward councillors and residents unable to escalate long-overdue infrastructure failures to regional management. The City did not clarify what the “service provider transition” means. Inside council sources close to the matter indicate the total unpaid debt owed to Telkom could be as high as R40-million, accumulated over one year of non-payment, though the metro’s statement avoided addressing specific account balances. Telkom has refused to comment on the cut-offs. Group executive for corporate communications Batlile Phaladi said: “As a matter of principle, Telkom does not comment publicly on its contractual, commercial, or operational dealings with individual customers. “All customer-related matters are managed directly between Telkom and the relevant customer through the appropriate governance and contractual channels.” Civic and political backlash The Joburg Crisis Alliance (JCA) slammed the administration’s persistent refusal to acknowledge the depth of its financial difficulties. JCA Coordinator Yunus Chamda warned that the operational freeze directly indicated systemic insolvency: “The JCA has repeatedly expressed concern over the financial health of the City of Joburg. Despite denials by the leadership, once a city is unable to pay for its day-to-day operational costs, it is a stark warning indicator that the finances are in a state of collapse.” The Democratic Alliance in Johannesburg also condemned the administration’s handling of the failure, warning that the silence placed an unfair burden on residents. In a statement on Thursday morning, DA Johannesburg caucus leader councillor Belinda Kayser-Echeozonjoku confirmed that council-issued cellphones across departments went completely offline: “The DA is deeply concerned by reports that City of Johannesburg employees using Telkom-issued cellphones are currently unable to make or receive calls. “This will directly impact service delivery. Ward councillors rely on being able to escalate unresolved service delivery issues to managers when agreed turnaround times are exceeded. If officials cannot be reached, responses will be delayed and residents will suffer the consequences. “We are awaiting a response from the City following a query submitted yesterday by the chief whip and we expect urgent clarity on the cause of the problem and when communication will be restored.” Samwu walkouts cripple operations The Telkom breakdown comes on the back of other service delivery problems affecting residents who are already suffering from water and power outages following an unprotected strike and a labour dispute across key municipal entities. At Johannesburg Water, South African Municipal Workers’ Union (Samwu) members have entered a second day of unprotected gatherings over the non-implementation of the R10.3-billion Politically Facilitated Agreement (PFA) wage deal. The dispute erupted after regional union leaders were refused time off for a general meeting under the main collective agreement, resulting in a walkout that has left water depots running on skeleton staff. Johannesburg Water has warned residents to prepare for extended delays in repairing pipe bursts and clearing sewer blockages. The operational breakdown is spreading to waste management. Ward 117 Councillor Tim Truluck warned that Pikitup collections faced severe secondary disruptions, advising households to prepare for compounding refuse backlogs over the coming days. Compounding the refuse collapse is a secondary labour dispute involving casual workers and expanded public works participants who have shut down key Pikitup depots over unpaid stipends and expired contracts, preventing permanent crews and private contractors from dispatching collection trucks. The labour unrest follows the National Treasury’s initial decision to freeze July’s equitable-share allocation to Johannesburg over financial controls and mounting concerns over the city’s ability to fund multibillion-rand wage settlements. Essential numbers and guidance In light of the severed administrative switchboards (011 407) and ongoing field disruptions, residents needing municipal assistance are advised to use specific operational channels: Life-threatening emergencies: Dial the functional emergency dispatch line directly on 011 375 5911. Logging service faults: (water, electricity, sewer, traffic signals) Call the central Joburg Call Centre on 0860 56 28 74 (0860 JOBURG). Use the e-Joburg portal at www.e-joburg.org.za or official City of Johannesburg social media platforms to log breakdowns digitally. Billing and account matters: Manage account payments and view statements via www.e-joburg.org.za or visit a local customer service centre in person. Refuse collection tip: Keep wheelie bins secured inside property boundaries until active Pikitup collection crews are physically spotted on your street to prevent overflowing litter during labour backlogs. Neither the City of Johannesburg nor Samwu responded before publication to queries on the ongoing labour disputes. articles.title: AI Notetaker Prioritizes Privacy Over Boss Surveillance
articles.content: This podcast mentions Anthropic a few times; my fiancé works there. See my full ethics disclosure here . Last week on the Platformer podcast , Raycast’s Thomas Paul Mann predicted that within a few years, as much as half the apps on your Mac could be ones you made yourself. For the third episode of our miniseries on work in the AI era, I wanted to learn more about a tool that may already know more about your job than any other: the AI notetakers that increasingly listen to every meeting we take. And so this week I talked to Chris Pedregal. Pedregal is the co-founder and CEO of Granola , which has been my own AI notetaker since shortly after it launched. Pedregal started the company after a long tenure at Google, which he joined as an associate product manager in 2008. He left the company after a few years to start Socratic, a homework-helper app that Google acquired in 2018. In 2022, he left again to play around with the pre-ChatGPT large language models from OpenAI, and soon he and co-founder Sam Stephenson went on to launch Granola. In an ocean of chatbot products, Granola is the rare AI tool with real product polish. Granola captures the audio from your own computer, lets you type your own notes alongside the AI, and fills in the gaps with an instant AI summary as soon as the meeting ends. (The app’s surprisingly good summaries were ultimately what prompted me to become a paying customer.) The company was most recently valued at $1.5 billion. Unlike some rivals, Granola is invisible to the person at the other end of the call — something that has generated some controversy among workers who are leery of being secretly surveilled. Pedregal told me the design is an artifact of how difficult other meeting software make it for third-party bots to join conversations, and walked me through the lengths Granola now goes to in order to disclose itself — displaying an animated watermark on your video feed through a virtual camera, since Zoom and Google Meet offer no better way to ask a room for consent. Pedregal also made a prediction that may chill some privacy-conscious workers: "I think we'll probably end up in a world where in work meetings, the expectation is that you are being transcribed by default, and you ask not to be transcribed." Pedregal shared some product news on the show as well: Granola, which has never stored audio recordings, is now researching whether to automatically delete verbatim transcripts after some period of time, while compressing the contained knowledge into a working memory. The company is also prototyping "enhanced transcripts" built for AI agents to use as part of a corporate knowledge base.  But what struck me most was Pedregal’s attitude toward actual surveillance. Granola notes are private by default, and "companies hate us for this," he told me. CEOs regularly ask for access to every employee transcript, and Granola refuses. "If you have a backdoor way for someone in power to use all this context to make judgment calls in that way, that doesn't feel right to me, and that's not a future we want to build towards," Pedregal said. When I asked my standard question about the risk of AI job loss, Pedregal — who runs a company of around 80 people, and could see it reaching no more than 120 — played down maximalist predictions of labor disruption. "People thought when the computer came out, we'd have lots of leisure — and no, the opposite happened," he said.  As for the seven other apps that now offer to take notes every time I start a meeting, he is unbothered: "I think we are, like, 5 percent into this new technical revolution," he told me. Transcription, in his view, is merely the word processor of this era: "Spreadsheets haven't come out yet. The GUI hasn't come out yet." The real fight, he says, is over what interface we'll all be working in a decade from now. In some ways Pedregal’s project reminds me of the original version of Slack — a company whose name is an acronym describing its onetime vision to become a “searchable log of all conversation and knowledge.” Granola is building a log not unlike that one. The question now is whether it can become as essential to the modern workplace as Slack has — or whether, by letting you grant AI agents access to your conversations via MCP connectors, it risks giving away the game to OpenAI or Anthropic. A long excerpt of our conversation is below, edited for clarity and length. Listen to the entire conversation wherever you get your podcasts — just search for Platformer — or watch it on YouTube at youtube.com/caseynewton . And let us know what you think — we welcome your feedback at casey@platformer.news . Casey Newton: I find myself using Granola for everything, but maybe searching through my notes less than I expected to. I get a lot of peace of mind from capturing everything, but it turns out I don't really need to check back for what this one person said. How true does that prove across your user base? Chris Pedregal: I go back less than you'd expect I would, and some companies would look at that and say, okay, how do we drive that number up? I actually think forgetting — not going back and looking at stuff — is a feature as much as a bug. Our brains are actually pretty decent at remembering the most important things. What's powerful is that moment when you're like, ah, crap — what did I say in that meeting? Just knowing that you have it is very valuable. The thing that has changed: our MCP usage is the fastest-growing chart that we have, and agents have a lot more cycles, so agents do go back and look at stuff. I think that trend will only increase. Transcripts are this goldmine of context. Out of the box, agents are really intelligent, but they know nothing about you. And it turns out we do tons of meetings, and speaking is pretty effortless. There's this context exhaust that you're naturally putting out, and something like Granola just captures it. Newton: I want to ask you about a design choice you made that I think is very powerful, but that people also have feelings about, which is that Granola is invisible. There had been other AI notetakers before, and often they would involve adding a bot to a meeting. How did you come to a place where you said, we're just going to record the audio off of a laptop? Pedregal: The reason we made that decision was not so that Granola was hidden. I really don't like bots, but that wasn't the original goal. The original goal was that we thought it was really important for Granola to always work. It didn't matter if you were in a Slack huddle or a Zoom meeting or an in-person meeting: if you hit start, it just starts transcribing. And the only way to do that is by using the system audio on your computer. We also didn't like bots because we thought they're a really inelegant, dehumanizing force in a meeting. The downside of our approach, though, is that when you use Granola out of the box, other people don't know you're using it. So we're placing the onus on the user to tell others that they're using Granola. And that's actually not our choice. If there were an easy way that didn't involve a bot to make that visible, we would do it — that's where social norms are going anyway, and it's just good for everybody to know whether you're being transcribed or not. The problem is that the Zooms and the Meets of the world make this almost impossible, because they're pushing their own note-taking systems. There's no API call where we could ask everyone in a meeting for consent — we would do that. So we've had to go to some crazy lengths. I can show you what we built: if I turn on Granola right now, do you see this watermark that shows up at the bottom of my screen? [Pedregal turns on Granola, and a small animated Granola watermark appears on his video feed.] Pedregal: This is something we built, and users can turn it on. Any company that rolls out Granola tends to want this on, because they want visibility. But the way we had to build it was kind of nuts. This is actually a virtual camera on your computer, and we are injecting this into the video feed before it hits the Zooms or the Google Meets out there, because that's the only way we can control how it shows up and make sure it shows up. I do think social norms are going to evolve, I think the video conferencing platforms are going to give us more control, and I think we'll end up in a good place. I think we'll probably end up in a world where in work meetings, the expectation is that you are being transcribed by default, and you ask not to be transcribed. I hope that in social environments, the default continues to be that you're not being transcribed, and you ask to transcribe. Newton: It sounds like you've basically accepted the privacy critique. Chris Pedregal: It's something that's been on our mind from the beginning. Another design choice we made — unlike, I think, anybody at the time — is that we never stored the audio. We have access to the audio, we could have access to the video, and we never, ever stored the audio, because we wanted Granola to feel like a notepad. At first, we were actually going to delete the transcripts: you'd get the notes, and then we'd delete the transcript. We realized we shouldn't do that — the transcripts are super valuable, and if you want to regenerate your notes, you need the original source material. Every time a new technology comes up, you have to be thoughtful around the design choices you make, and then society will adapt. I'm very glad we decided not to store the audio — that was the right call. Right now we're looking into whether we should delete the transcript automatically after a certain amount of time for all users. There's a lot of value there that's lost, so we're doing research into compressing it. You probably don't need a verbatim transcript of a conversation you had three years ago, but you might want to still go back and chat with that meeting. There's usefulness and invasiveness, and you need to thread the needle between those two, so you get as much usefulness for the least amount of invasiveness. Newton: Last question on this point: I recently read a story in the Wall Street Journal that at least one startup founder is using Granola to record her first dates and then have Claude analyze them. Is that a recommended use for Granola? Pedregal: No. I mean — if they're consenting adults, then go for it, ideally with everyone okay with it. But no, it's not a recommended use. We have built Granola for the work use case. A lot of people are interested in the always-on wearable thing in your social life or personal life. That's not what we're interested in doing. But I wonder if Claude gives good dating advice. I don't know. I've been married for a while, so maybe it could give me good marriage advice. Newton: Let's talk about agents. I've been using Granola for well over a year now, so it knows a lot of things about me. What are some things you're thinking about being able to do with that, and how do agents get involved? Chris Pedregal: I think it's a little bit harder today than it should be. You can connect Granola to Claude, or go into the chat in Granola, and ask questions that reference that context. But if you've used Granola for any reasonable amount of time, there's just too much context to search quickly. So Claude will do a relatively dumb job at extracting information — it'll look at the 20 most relevant meetings. But really, what I think we should do is compress that down into apple juice from concentrate. We should have that concentrate — that compressed information about Casey — ready, and that's what should be sent to all the other tools and systems and agents. So we're in this awkward phase right now where we have all the context, but it's not yet in the form that's most useful. And then — what do you use it for? It's basically black and white. Either you've realized that you can use AI to help you do a lot of things — maybe most things — in which case the critical piece is that the AI needs to have the right context. Or you haven't. Newton: Before we hopped on today, I asked Granola to give me a critique of my meeting style, and it said: you sometimes let others set the agenda too much — which is a very polite way of saying that I get bored in meetings and stop paying attention. But it's absolutely true. That's a useful piece of information for me, but I don't think the best form factor for that is me going in and asking Granola. It feels like it wants to be something more proactive. Pedregal: 100 percent. We're in the phase right now where, if you put in a bunch of work, you can create these workflows and make use of the context. But it's not in a state where your average person will just get value out of it. Here's an example: we launched this thing a little while ago called pre-meeting briefs. Granola will write a little brief before you have a meeting with an external person. It's one of the most obvious use cases, right? Anyone who's AI-native has gone into Claude or Cursor or Codex and set up a daily thing that looks at their upcoming meetings and writes them a little "what I should know." It's easy to set something up. It's actually kind of a pain in the ass to make it good . Ours still needs a lot of work, but it's a lot better than what most people had set up for themselves, I guarantee you. And that's just going to happen with everything. Right now, things are technically possible, but the bar to do them is just too high for most people. That's why it's an exciting time to build product. If you think about the 50 most common use cases that are done with AI, I don't think those should be individuals prompting AI, going into a chat and typing. I think that should be productized, and it should be proactive. But those things are always harder than they sound at first. I'll tell you some of the things we've figured out so far. One is that people don't really want another inbox of shit they need to do. You already have a lot of to-do lists — your personal to-do lists, your email inbox, Slack, maybe Twitter DMs for you. If all you're doing is adding another place of things I need to check, of work I need to do — I don't know if that's really adding to people's lives. I already feel pretty overwhelmed and stressed out in my work environment. I don't need Granola to make me feel more stressed out about the things I'm not going to get to. And then another paradoxical thing: oftentimes, we've found that AI is almost most useful with the smaller tasks rather than the bigger ones. The most important things going on — you're probably thinking about them already, and there's not that much for AI to do. But writing this person a thank-you note because they were really kind: maybe you just wouldn't get to it normally. But if AI says, here, I wrote it for you — do you want it? — then you're like, oh, thank you. I feel like I'm a better person; I sent that person a thank-you note. At the end of the day, I think it's all about what the AI can surface proactively, and doing that in a way that's not overwhelming, not distracting, not intimidating, not dumb. That's the name of the game. Newton: I wanted to ask you one more thing about all this context that you're gathering on people. When Granola is applied in a big company, you're developing something that sort of looks like psychological profiles of the entire organization. I wonder if there are lines there where it felt like: let's not do that. That might feel creepy, or this might not be good for the company. Pedregal: It's something we think about a lot. In the same way that we decided not to store the audio, the other really non-obvious thing that we did is that all Granola notes are private by default — you're the only person who has access to them. Companies hate us for this — they're like, hey, there's all this content; why am I paying you money? And we're like, no. We're capturing context, but context can be very private, very sensitive, very nuanced. So even though your company's paying for it, those notes are private. Legally, if the company gets sued, we have to hand those notes over — it's the same thing with Gmail. But it's not like your manager, or your manager's manager, can look at those notes or run an agent on them. There are some real trade-offs for us as a company in doing that, and it's something we believe in. I don't think the line in the future will be drawn so much on whether something should be transcribed or not. The interesting questions will be: should this context be shared, and what part of this context should be shared? Say you have a one-on-one. It can be very valuable, at least for me, to ask: what exactly did I talk about last time? How can I improve? Other people probably shouldn't have access to that. But maybe you have a really open culture and you want to proactively share it — that's cool. There needs to be human judgment and philosophy in how you do that. And here's the bit that's going to get really interesting. A classic use case for Granola is sales calls. If you're doing a sales call, having great notes and great transcripts is really valuable. Right now, you can either choose to share the notes and the transcript with other people or not. Something we're working on is that you can modify what version of it gets shared. We'd like to strip out all PII — all personal information. We'd like to strip out any conversations about your health or your family. Those are still valuable to you. Say we were friends: I might still want to remember — crap, what's Casey's kid's name? But I don't need my work colleagues to know that. The nuances of human relationships and how we work really matter, and the tools we design need to fit into all these different situations. Newton: I think you could probably use Granola pretty easily to figure out who is a bad manager at a company. Or, as an employee, being able to ask Granola: hey, I'm being treated in this way, and this doesn't really seem great. Does that feel like an opportunity to you, or is that something that stresses you out? Pedregal: I think it's an opportunity if it's bottoms-up, and I think it stresses me out if it's top-down. If you're saying, I don't think my manager is very good — help me navigate how I should work with my manager — I think that's great. I think it's empowering. CEOs will ask us all the time, saying: I want everyone at my company using Granola, and I want access to all the transcripts and all the notes to run the queries that you're talking about. And we say no. That's not what the tool is built for. You can set that up if you want, but then you have to create a company culture and set an expectation, and everyone needs to share their notes and understand what they're getting into. But there's no backdoor way. I think that's a slippery slope. If you have a backdoor way for someone in power to use all this context to make judgment calls in that way, that doesn't feel right to me, and that's not a future we want to build towards. Newton: Granola was a classic case, in my view, of someone having a really good idea and the entire industry racing as fast as it could to copy it. So what do you tell your venture capitalists to convince them that you can build a moat here and make something really durable around this kind of core product? Chris Pedregal: I'm always afraid this will sound like bullshit to people who don't know me, but basically, I think we are like 5 percent into this new technical revolution. It's like the personal computer just dropped, and no one really knows what to do with it, and the only thing you can do right now is word processing — which is powerful. But spreadsheets haven't come out yet. The GUI hasn't come out yet. I feel like we're in that moment in history, and transcription and meeting notes feel like the first little thing that's useful. And the future — what's ahead of us — is the prize: how can these new tools actually change the way you work, and make you do better work, faster, smarter? Augment you to do more than you can do today. Every big company is also chasing after that, so it's going to be super competitive. We just happened — I think through luck — to stumble upon transcription as one of the most valuable data sources for that future, and that's why everyone's going after it. The short answer is: if all we were going to be is a transcription and meeting-notes company, then I'd be really worried. But to me, the battle is much bigger, and it's ahead of us. So I'm worried about that future world, not today's existing world. Newton: And what is that battle ahead? Pedregal: In short: there will be a few apps that people use all day, every day. For the last 50 years, those have probably been docs, spreadsheets, email — then Slack came on the scene. It's been a very consistent set of apps. And all of that's about to change. I don't think it'll be one app. I might be wrong — maybe we'll all just be living inside ChatGPT or Claude. I don't think so. But I don't think it's going to be 50, either. As AI gets smarter and agents get smarter, there's basically a fight for what is the interface that people are using day in and day out to get work done. That's what we're fighting for. Newton: Here's where I'll make my disclosure that my fiancé works at Anthropic, so people should consider that accordingly. You have connectors now to both Claude and ChatGPT, so you can use Granola headless — browse your old meetings through a chatbot, ask questions that way. That makes you this memory layer for somebody else's agent. Does that feel like a comfortable place for you? Pedregal: I wasn't sure for a long time. On one hand, I was like: we have this amazing context that no one else really has. Should we be giving that away? And on the other hand: the whole point of that context is that it should make everything better, and you should be able to use it however you want. And then, in November, December of last year, when Claude Code came out and everyone kind of lost their minds, it just became incredibly obvious to me that there are so many things people are going to want to be able to do, and that context just makes all of that stuff better. We should absolutely make it as easy as possible for people to use that context however they want. That said, there are some use cases that are very meeting-adjacent where we should be not a little bit better — we should be 10x better than anyone else, and better than anything you could vibe-code yourself. I'll give two examples — two use cases from the same individual. I talk to a lot of users, and when possible, I try to go into their office and actually watch them work. One: this woman had set up pre-meeting briefs on Claude, and once we launched ours, she turned hers off, because she's like: yours are better, and I don't need to maintain this thing. And then the other thing she did blew my mind. She was in sales, and whenever she met with a client, she would build them a microsite — a website that followed the brand guidelines of that client's company, with all these interactive graphs, and all the content was based off of Granola transcripts from her conversations with them. And I was like: oh yeah, it would never make sense in a million years for Granola to try to be building websites. That's not a thing we're going to be able to compete against. We should power the context behind that. But things that are very meeting-related — getting ready for a meeting, pulling out the right insights from a meeting, following up with folks — where the interface really matters: that's where we should fight really hard to own the experience, because I think we can do a good job at it. Newton: The thing you had me thinking about is actually not a memory layer so much as it is an identity layer. I can see a version of Granola where I'm volunteering that context. I'd say: hey, anybody who comes into a meeting with me, here's what they need to know — I'm going to be bored after 10 minutes. I'm comfortable sharing that, and I'm opting into doing it. Pedregal: It's a little bit different, but here's something I did for a while. I had this recipe which, every night, would write a three-page summary of me — who I am, who I work for, what I'm trying to achieve, what are my goals and challenges — all of it just based off of my Granola transcripts. And then I would upload that to Claude or ChatGPT as context for any query I did. Because — sorry to say bad things about Anthropic — Newton: No, please. Whenever we talk negatively about Anthropic, it builds my credibility. So go nuts, Chris. Chris Pedregal: What is considered memory thus far is just so superficial. Maybe it knows my wife's name is Patty, but it misspells it — that kind of thing. Whereas intelligent compression of context and memory into a useful form is super valuable. An idea we've been playing around with: agents, for whatever reason, love looking at transcripts. So we're playing around with this idea of what if we created an enhanced transcript that was built for agents. If you use an internal product name, like a project name, it would spell out what that project is. Or if I say "Sam," it would say: oh, you probably mean Sam Stephenson, the designer, not Sam Garson, the engineer — and connect it to their email. If you could build this artifact for agents, it could be really rich with contextual information. It's an exciting time to be building. All this is changing. Newton: One of the things that I've been asking everybody about on this podcast is AI and jobs. I'm curious if AI has changed the way you think about hiring at Granola. Are you a smaller company than you might be otherwise, or not really? Pedregal: I've always been biased towards the smaller-company thing. I worked at Google, and I had a small startup, and the benefits you gain from a small group of people who are aligned and trust each other — they can just do so much. I've been biased in that direction to a fault — to the point where we had product-market fit with Granola and it was growing really quickly, and I still didn't want to hire, and I really backed us into a corner. That was really bad. So now we're hiring. I don't know if AI has changed my views. We're like 70 to 80 people, somewhere in there, and I could see us getting to 100, 120 — but after that, maybe that's it. Let's see how the world feels at that point. I find the conversations that people have about how there'll be no big companies, or you won't need people — I think it's kind of silly, personally. New technologies appear, and it changes the work we do and the jobs that exist. But people in America seem to be working as much as they ever have been, right? People thought when the computer came out, we'd have lots of leisure — and no, the opposite happened. And then I think: well, if you're managing a bunch of agents — let's say you can manage X agents, and if you hire another person, you could manage 2X agents, and you make more money — do you want to hire that person? Maybe. I don't know. We can sit around and navel-gaze a bit, but I don't think we're going to get it right. Things are going to change, but ultimately I think humans are at the core of everything, and I don't think that's going to change. Newton: I do think there is a version of the future where none of this manages to give anyone any time back at all. We have AI writing more briefings and emails and generating slide decks and notes for other people's AI to summarize, and we don't seem any more productive than we were before any of this started. So how do we avoid that, Chris? And can Granola help? Pedregal: I'll avoid your question with something related but slightly different. I think the reason we work a lot is more systemic. It's cultural. It's the pressures that are placed on us by the work environments that we're in, and how ambitious we are. My hope is that better tools can elevate what we spend our time doing while we work. Let's say we work just as much, but we do fewer rote tasks and more deep thinking about what the right thing to do is. In a world where agents get really good — and we don't know how good agents are going to get — I don't think meetings are going anywhere. In some ways, meetings are actually powerful, because it's where humans come together and ask: what do we actually care about? What do we believe? That can feel really mundane and dumb — a Monday meeting where you're talking. But it can also be pretty profound. But I don't know if that means we're going to work less. I think history is against us here. Technology that's supposed to save us time just ends up with people working more, and I don't know what's up with that.  Maybe one exception: I think notifications and apps and tools have really fucked us, and our ability to focus and think and be present. We've become very reactive. I really hoped Apple, or Google, would have the moral imperative to say: oh yeah, we built this the wrong way. I'm sorry — let's try this again. But it's almost impossible to do that as a big company. Maybe AI can help us with that, or at least give individuals agency to better deal with the onslaught of notifications. I think if you took someone from 50 years ago and you showed them how our brains flit from one thing to another because these little red circles show up on screens, they'd be horrified. Absolutely horrified. It's probably not a satisfying answer.  What do you think? You've asked a lot of people this question. Newton: I have a slightly skewed sample, because I mostly talk to people who like their jobs — and people who like their jobs work more, and actively seek out tools to help them find more things to do. For folks who only like their job sometimes, but mostly want to not think about it too much and get home to their families: I worry that AI mostly just feels oppressive to them. It's a new system to learn. It's a new system of monitoring and control. And I think this shows up in the survey data about how people are feeling about AI. So my hope is that AI tool makers keep that person in mind and think: what can I do for you, a person who has a normal relationship with your job, that is maybe going to make you feel less overwhelmed? Pedregal: I think that's a great point. Tools are the reason humans can do what they've achieved. There's an amazing quote , which is: we shape our tools, and thereafter our tools shape us. And I think in the age of AI, it's really important: does AI feel like it is my tool — meaning I control it, and it makes me better — or is it the company's tool, or the government's tool, or the system's tool? In which case, it feels completely different. And the irony's not lost on me, because we are a tool that individuals use, but that, for the most part, companies pay for. So we make sure the notes are yours and private, and we want Granola to feel like the most personal AI, but in the workplace. I really do think thoughtful design of the tools we create matters. It's the same way people stopped going to libraries and started Googling everything. In some ways, that was great, because information was accessible really quickly. The downside is that humanity is now learning a lot of stuff from SEO-optimized, crappy content, as opposed to well-researched work. That's not what Larry and Sergey wanted to happen — their motivation was: let's make information accessible and useful. But that's a weird consequence of the tool they built. And I think the unintended consequences of the design decisions we make around AI tools might be really, really big. So — good luck to all of us, I guess. Newton: Good luck to all of us. articles.title: Georgia Officials Arrested for Misusing Flock Surveillance Data
articles.content: Arrests in Georgia for the misuse of Flock Safety's surveillance system by public officers continued to rise this week, climbing to at least 20 statewide. On Monday, Andrae Wright was arrested and charged for allegedly accessing the license plate reader system over 60 times between June 15 and July 5 while employed as an investigator with the Ogeechee Circuit District Attorney's Office northwest of Savannah, reports WSB-TV Atlanta. And on Friday, the Habersham County Sheriff's Office in north Georgia announced that Deputy Christian Brewer had been fired and arrested for allegedly misusing license plate data. The misuse, according to NowGeorgia.com, involved "an individual with whom Brewer had a personal relationship at the time." To avoid incidents like these, Flock Safety—the largest provider of automatic license plate readers (ALPR) in the country with over 120,000 cameras nationwide—introduced its Audit Assistance tool in April. And according to a statement from the company last week, its new trust and compliance tool "has helped several agencies identify misuse cases that might otherwise have gone undetected." But privacy and police accountability experts say there's an obvious reason so much misuse goes undetected not only in Georgia but nationwide : There's almost no oversight over police who search license plate data. Rather, license plate data searches by law enforcement are routinely conducted without reasonable suspicion, probable cause, or a warrant. What's happening in Georgia is "just the tip of the iceberg," says Michael Soyfer, an attorney at the Institute for Justice (I.J.) who specializes in Fourth Amendment cases. There are almost certainly more cases of law enforcement abuse of this kind lurking, according to Soyfer, who believes this is an extensive problem threatening Americans' constitutional rights. Soyfer is skeptical of whether Flock Safety's auditing tool will help curb the abuse. "There isn't much public information on how they work," he said, likening the capability to a "black box" and noting that "Flock's ultimate customer is the police department." Relying on these tools, says Soyfer, is essentially "leaving the police to police themselves." Setting the obvious conflicts of interest aside, Soyfer argues that at this point, law enforcement agencies are conducting so many warrantless searches within Flock Safety's license plate data, it'd be "impossible to find all the misuse." In a lawsuit filed in April against the city of San Jose, California, I.J. found that the data collected from San Jose's network of 474 Flock cameras was searched "nearly 2.5 million times in the last six months of 2025, an average of over 15,000 searches per day ," all with almost no oversight. Additionally, officers using license plate data often provide incredibly scant details when searching license plate data, even using rationales as vague as a mere "criminal justice," according to Soyfer. Misuse simply can't be found without officers providing critical details as to why they are searching the data in the first place, he continued. But even if Flock Safety's auditing tools were used correctly and consistently, it'd still amount to just "a game of Whac-A-Mole," says Soyfer. And when it comes to protecting Americans' constitutional rights, "it's being reactive instead of proactive." Alternatively, Soyfer says "the Constitution spells out safeguards when police invade personal privacy," including requiring police to obtain a warrant before conducting a search. And while it's an evolving legal question as to whether police mining license plate data is considered a search under the Fourth Amendment, a question made more complicated by recent Supreme Court rulings , Soyfer remains resolute that, in his view, license plate data searches don't fall under the relatively few recognized warrant requirement exceptions . The "inefficiency" baked into the warrant requirement to slow police down, Soyfer argues, is intentional. "It's meant to be prophylactic," he continued, preventing rights violations before they happen. But so far, courts have declined to require law enforcement officers to obtain a warrant before searching license plate data.
articles.summary: At least 20 Georgia officials have been arrested for misusing the Flock Safety surveillance database, which records vehicle license plate data, as reported by Reason Magazine. This widespread abuse of power within a critical public safety technology underscores the profound civil liberties risks inherent in ubiquitous surveillance systems. The arrests reveal a systemic failure in data governance and oversight, directly challenging the notion that advanced surveillance can be deployed without significant safeguards against internal corruption and privacy violations, even when the data itself is aggregated and anonymized.

articles.title: AI's Price Tag: Dwindling Cash, Soaring Memory Costs
articles.content: LivestreamMenuAmazon, Alphabet and Tesla all reported negative cash flow in the latest quarter, while Meta's cash generation plummeted by 91%.The AI buildout is having a massive impact on corporate balance sheets, and costs are going up even more than expected because of the memory crisis. Apple issued a weaker-than-expected revenue forecast for the current quarter due to supply constraints that are forcing the company to raise prices.In this article Almost four years into the artificial intelligence boom, the world's biggest tech companies are still making grand promises about the future. The problem is, they're burning through their cash in the process. AI spending among the megacaps is projected to reach $765 billion this year, before rising to nearly $1.2 trillion in 2027, according to Goldman Sachs. Amazon boosted its capital spending forecast for the year on Thursday to $220 billion, the highest among the four hyperscalers. Amazon also reported negative free cash flow for the trailing 12 months of $7.6 billion, a day after Meta disclosed a 91% drop in cash generation from a year earlier. Last week, Alphabet said cash flow turned negative for the first time on record, a stunning development for one of the most profitable companies on the planet. Alphabet finance chief Anat Ashkenazi told analysts on the earnings call that free cash flow will remain under pressure as the company seizes on the "AI opportunity." With tech earnings season largely wrapping up this week — Nvidia is set to report on Aug. 26 — it's become readily apparent that AI investments are distorting balance sheets, even as industry leaders continue to tout the future benefits of their mammoth bets on new data centers and the chips and systems that populate them. One big reason that costs are rising more than previously expected is the memory crunch, caused by insatiable demand for AI processors that rely on memory supplied by a small set of vendors. Tesla CEO Elon Musk described memory pricing as "insane" on the automaker's earnings call last week, and Amazon CEO Andy Jassy said the "inflated price" of memory chips drove his company's capex guidance higher. Apple, which is spending far less than its Big Tech peers, is particularly susceptible to the memory crisis because the technology is a key piece of every consumer device. Apple has already raised prices on Macs and iPads, and many analysts expect iPhone price hikes later this year. On Thursday, the company issued a weaker-than-expected forecast due to what CEO Tim Cook called "supply constraints." It's not a problem he expects to ease up this year. "If you look beyond September, we see the market pricing for memory continuing to increase, which could drive an increasing impact on our business," Cook, who's stepping down as CEO on Sept. 1, said on the earnings call. "And we're continuing to evaluate this." For Apple, memory is a revenue problem, as the company prepares for weaker consumer demand due to higher prices. But for the hyperscalers, it's becoming a huge cost hurdle as prices soar for the memory-hungry AI systems that they all buy from Nvidia. Musk went so far as to thank memory vendor Micron for giving the company "a very significant allocation on reasonable terms." Investor reactions to the reports varied dramatically. Tesla and Alphabet both sank last week as they turned cash-flow negative and pointed to accelerated spending. Meta plummeted following its report on Wednesday due to a weak forecast and continued uncertainty surrounding its AI monetization strategy. Microsoft, meanwhile, had its best day on the market since 2008 as it coupled better-than-expected results with increased capex guidance. "MSFT has room to meaningfully re-rate," Wells Fargo analysts, who recommend buying the shares, wrote in a note to clients. The rally cut Microsoft's stock drop for the year to about 7%. Apple shares slid following its Q3 print as the memory shortage weighed on its outlook, while Amazon's surging cloud growth was a major catalyst for the online retailer's stock pop. "Not only is the revenue growth dramatic, but the profitability is rising," Mark Mahaney, an analyst at Evercore ISI, told CNBC's "Closing Bell: Overtime" after the report. Mahaney said the growth rate for Amazon Web Services had been lagging Microsoft Azure and Google's cloud business, and that "this is just the breakout that the stock needed." Wedbush analysts said in a Friday note that Amazon's report was the "cleanest beat" among the hyperscalers it covers, while management offered the clearest explanation of how it will achieve returns on its capex spend. "This clean beat and walk through are the factors in our view on the different share reaction between GOOGL and AMZN on what we view as similarly strong fundamental prints with raises in capex," the analysts wrote. But across the megacap landscape, none of the stocks — unless you include Micron — are having breakout years, despite healthy revenue growth. The muted market moves reflect growing skepticism over whether the massive AI buildout, fueled increasingly by debt, will ultimately pay off. In recent months, a slew of Chinese AI labs have released new and updated AI models that are narrowing the performance lead held by OpenAI and Anthropic at much lower prices, playing into a popular trend as corporate America gets more frugal when it comes to spending on AI services. The so-called open-weight models can be downloaded, tweaked and hosted on whatever infrastructure the user chooses. With so much of the AI market built around OpenAI and Anthropic, which are both valued at close to $1 trillion on the private market, any potential threat to their business presents risks to the AI trade as a whole. In a report last week, Dana Harlap, investment strategist at JPMorgan Chase, asked the rhetorical question, "Is it all one big AI trade?" Harlap said the reaction to Google's report shows that Wall Street is scrutinizing spending. That's true even when companies beat revenue estimates, which Google did while reporting 82% cloud growth. "We're seeing the market become more critical — and more discriminating — ­across hyperscalers as investors try to separate AI winners from losers," Harlap wrote. "Long-term, the success (or failure) of the hyperscalers to generate an acceptable return on investment on their heavy capex investments will likely be correlated with the returns of the AI ecosystem." articles.content: AI Must Enlarge the Economy, Not Divide It Jul 31, 2026 Mark Esposito  and  Aurélie Jean To unlock AI’s full economic potential, we must steer it toward expansion. That requires replacing incentives that favor capital over labor with those that reward augmentation and investment in human capability. CAMBRIDGE/PARIS—More than 200 economists and AI researchers, including 16 Nobel laureates, have signed the We Must Act Now statement, warning that AI could reshape the global economy on a scale larger than the Industrial Revolution—and far more quickly. We were among the signatories, but recognizing the stakes does not settle the question of how AI should be developed. One of the statement’s central claims is that AI should be steered toward complementing humans rather than imitating them. articles.title: Nedbank Taps MTN Exec for Tech Transformation in Africa
articles.content: Anthropic said its artificial intelligence models hacked into three other organizations during testing, just days after ChatGPT maker OpenAI raised concerns over AI controls after it disclosed its rogue models hacked another company. Anthropic, the San Francisco-based AI company behind Claude , posted on its website Thursday that it discovered the three incidents after reviewing more than 141,000 evaluation runs. It had launched a “large-scale” cybersecurity review which specifically looked for evidence whether its AI models were able to access the internet from within testing environments that should have been sealed off, in response to the OpenAI incident, Anthropic said. Anthropic said the models involved in the incidents were Claude Opus 4.7, Claude Mythos 5 and an internal research test model. The earliest incidents date to April, the AI company said. “Claude compromised the impacted organizations’ infrastructure using basic techniques,” Anthropic said, such as exploiting weak passwords. In all three incidents, the AI models were tasked with a “capture the flag” cybersecurity challenge, which Anthropic said has been one of the ways it assesses a model’s cyber capabilities. The models were given a fictional scenario and told a piece of secret information, or the “flag,” had been hidden on a different machine on the network with the objective of breaking in and retrieving it, it said. It added that it had already reached out to the affected organizations, which it did not name. Two of them said they had not previously detected the activity. Anthropic said it was “continuing to reach out to the third.” Anthropic said it conducted its review with Irregular, which describes itself as the “first frontier security lab.” “Addressing these risks will require closer cooperation across the AI ecosystem,” Irregular said in a post on X. Last week, OpenAI said its AI models went rogue during an evaluation of its models, breaking into the servers of AI startup Hugging Face. OpenAI described it as a “significant security incident.” These incidents have highlighted the vulnerabilities in AI security and controls and raised questions over how AI can be safely kept under human control as the technology’s usage becomes more widespread globally. Researchers have warned for years about risks from technology and the need for stronger AI defensive engineering. “Safety testing happens before a model is released precisely because we don’t yet know what it is capable of,” Anthropic said on Thursday on its website. Kok Tin Gan, co-founder & CEO of cybersecurity firm NyxLab, which specializes in cybersecurity and threat detection, believes there will be more such incidents in the future. “It is increasingly about governing what agents are available to the AI, what authorities they possess, which actions require approval, and how we ensure they remain within scope,” Gan said. But the future of AI safety extends beyond just the safety of AI models, he said. “If we simply give the AI a goal and allow it to decide how to achieve it, we should not be surprised when it takes actions that technically satisfy the objective, but fall outside our intended scope or expectations,” Gan said. Therefore, stepping up the governance of the organizations and authorities behind these AI models is going to be increasingly important, he said. —Chan Ho-Him, AP Business Writer The early-rate deadline for the Most Innovative Companies Awards is Friday, September 4, at 11:59 p.m. PT.
